### B-194 · C-HE-09 §3 lossy lane-id encoding (collision half) *(surfaced by out-of-family Codex r6 against U-HE-29, 2026-08-22; misclassification half fixed in the landing PR, collision half register-and-held)*

- **What it is.** `_loop_structured_col` STRIPS ` `, tab, newline, CR, `|` and `;` out of a lane id before writing it, because each of those corrupts the row or the parse (`|` splits the row, whitespace breaks the item-token split, `;` terminates the lane, newlines split the row across lines). The strip is destructive rather than an encoding, so two distinct legal ids differing only in stripped characters (`lane;evil`, `laneevil`) render identically — one lane can read as another.

- **Current state.** The MISCLASSIFICATION half is fixed at HEAD: `arc_exit_report._sanitize_lane` applies the identical strip to its own `.lane-id` before comparing, so a lane bearing those characters no longer has its own obligations classified as foreign. The collision itself is inherent to a lossy mapping and remains. Not exploitable at HEAD — lane ids are minted from a host+repo+random-suffix template that produces none of the stripped characters, so a colliding pair needs a hand-set `HARNESS_LANE_ID` or a worktree name carrying a separator.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) Decide the shape: REJECT unsafe ids at mint time (`reservations.py mint-lane-id`, where identity is created) plus a fail-closed writer, OR one reversible encoding (percent-escape the unsafe set); (2) move all three carriers in ONE commit — `_loop_structured_col`, `rowparse`, `arc_exit_report._sanitize_lane` — since a writer and reader disagreeing about the encoding is the same defect in a new place; (3) pin a witness that two ids differing only in unsafe characters cannot render the same lane.

### B-195 · U-HE-29 cutover-window concurrency vs a live pre-U-HE-29 writer *(surfaced by out-of-family Codex r8 against U-HE-29, 2026-08-22; register-and-held — (a) fails in the C-HE-09 §4 safe direction, (b) is not fixable from this side)*

- **What it is.** Two residual races in `loop_status_migrate`, both confined to the cutover window in which a checkout still running PRE-U-HE-29 code is actively writing. **(a)** The staleness check and the import append are not atomic, so a `RESOLVED-HIL` landing between them lets an imported legacy `DEFERRED-HIL` become physically last and reopen a just-answered gate. **(b)** A pre-U-HE-29 process holding an fd on the legacy inode keeps appending after the claim rename; a deferral written after the reduce hits EOF lands only in the `.migrated-*` archive, which no later pass inspects. A third instance of the same root cause was re-found at r9: the orphan fold reads the live file with `cat` and replaces it with `mv`, so a row appended between EOF and the rename sits on an inode the replacement unlinks.

- **Current state.** Held deliberately. (a)'s consequence is the SAFE direction under C-HE-09 §4 — over-skipping is safe, under-skipping re-loops — so the item merely stays in the skip-set and resurfaces at the next SessionStart for the operator to re-resolve; no data loss, no wrongly-retried gate. (b) cannot be closed from this side at all: the old writer takes none of our locks and holds the inode regardless of its name. Both windows close on their own once no pre-U-HE-29 checkout remains.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) For (a), hold the existing `.loop-status.lock` (the fd-8 flock the TTL pass already uses) across the check AND the conditional append so the decision and the write are one critical section; confirm the contention cost, given that lock is otherwise taken only by the TTL pass. (2) For (b), have later passes also scan `.migrated-*` archives for rows appended after their archive timestamp and re-import under the same staleness rule — the only mitigation available without the old writer's cooperation. (3) Re-assess whether either is worth building once the window has closed.

### B-196 · per-arc `todo_for_human` scoping needs a per-item lane SET *(surfaced by out-of-family Codex r3/r5/r11 against U-HE-29, 2026-08-22; register-and-held after three flips — HEAD annotates and never drops)*

- **What it is.** U-WT-03 says `todo_for_human` is what THIS arc leaves for a human, but since U-HE-29 the ledger is shared and `loop_pending_hil_list` returns every lane's open gates. Filtering to this lane was tried twice and hid a real row both times: excluding every lane != mine dropped this arc's own UNATTRIBUTED rows (`defer.sh` writes no lane; migrated rows carry `-`), and excluding only demonstrably-foreign lanes still hid rows because the reducer collapses by ITEM TOKEN — when two lanes defer the same item, only the last deferrer's row survives, so another lane's rendering can be the sole trace of an item this lane also has open.

- **Current state.** The rendered lane is not evidence of sole ownership, so no exclusion built on it is sound. At HEAD the function ANNOTATES and never drops: it states the lane split in the notes and lists every row. Over-reporting a sibling's obligation is the safe direction; hiding this arc's own gate in the record that closes it — immediately before worktree disposition — is not.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) Decide whether C-HE-09 §3's rendered form should carry the SET of deferring lanes (`[L1,L2] item — detail`); that is a spec change and routes through design-phase back-flow, not an execution-time edit. (2) If the rendering stays singular, decide whether `arc_exit_report` should make a SECOND query for per-item lane membership rather than reading the rendering — weighed against the one-parse-one-authority rule. (3) Either way, keep annotate-never-drop until the chosen mechanism can prove sole ownership.

### B-197 · worktree GC can reap mid-drain (`.migrating-*` inside the `.harness/` ignore class) *(surfaced by the merge-gate concurrency lens on #1426, 2026-08-22; register-and-held — the raced outcome EQUALS the pre-U-HE-29 baseline, so this PR narrows exposure rather than creating loss)*

- **What it is.** `loop_status_migrate` claims a legacy ledger by renaming it to `.harness/loop_status.md.migrating-*`. `_HOOK_REGEN_IGNORED` (`tools/hooks/lib.sh:479`) matches `\.harness/`, so `hook_worktree_local_state` reports the worktree CLEAN — and a concurrent `loop_gc_worktrees reap`, which takes a removal mutex the migration never acquires, can delete the worktree mid-drain. The restore-on-failure `mv` then no-ops on the vanished path and the row reaches neither the shared venue nor disk. A third instance (merge-gate re-gate): the orphan-FOLD step runs BEFORE the claim-first rename with no serialization of its own, so two migrators seeing the same dead-owner orphan can each fold+republish+re-claim it — a duplicate `DEFERRED-HIL` and two archives for one orphan. Safe-direction under §4 (never a false `RESOLVED-HIL`), so log-noise, but it shows the claim-first guarantee does not span the whole function. A fourth instance: `loop_resolve`'s pre-write byte offset narrows the search but cannot EXCLUDE a concurrent append — if this process's write fails while another appends a byte-identical row in the same window, the grep succeeds and a false "resolved" is reported. A second, lower finding: `arc_exit_report.append_ledger_row` verifies its write by substring-in-tail rather than from a pre-write byte offset, so under the shared venue a concurrent duplicate EXIT-REPORT row for the same PR could make it report success when its own append failed.

- **Current state.** Held, with a severity correction the lens did not make: `origin/main` **already** gitignores `.harness/loop_status.md` (`.gitignore:149`), so the GC already reaps worktrees holding open `DEFERRED-HIL` rows. The raced outcome therefore **equals the pre-U-HE-29 baseline**, while every un-raced drain is strictly better (rows become durable in the shared venue). This PR narrows the exposure and adds one interrupted-drain window; it does not create the loss.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) The fix is a **decomposition** of the ignore class, not a reversal of either prior decision: `.migrated-*` is a permanent archive and must STAY ignored (codex r5 P2 — untracked residue wedges the worktree GC forever), while `.migrating-*` is a transient in-flight claim that should block reap while its owner is alive; `_loop_pid_alive` already exists for that test. This edits shared GC machinery (`_HOOK_REGEN_IGNORED` / `hook_worktree_local_state`) with its own suites, which is why it was not improvised at merge time. (2) For the growth check, scope to a pre-write byte offset **and** add a per-call nonce — byte-offset scoping alone cannot distinguish a byte-identical concurrent row. (3) Re-assess once no pre-U-HE-29 checkout remains: the migration becomes dead code then and the window closes with it.

### B-198 · pre-U-HE-29 legacy ledgers carry nothing under their own semantics — no drain built *(measured during the U-HE-29 PR, 2026-08-22; the migration built there was CUT on this measurement, and B-195/B-197 closed with it)*

- **What it is.** U-HE-29 moved the HIL ledger to a shared venue (C-HE-09 §2). A cutover migration was built during that PR and then **cut before merge**, on measurement.

- **The measurement, recorded so nobody re-derives it.** Reducing a legacy per-worktree ledger with the NEW no-ACTIVATE-reset rule (C-HE-09 §4) is **not evidence** about what it holds — those rows were *written* under the old rule, where `ACTIVATE` cleared prior-run state. On this workspace the root checkout's ledger (3204 lines, 18 `ACTIVATE` rows) reduces to `B-124 B-137` under the new rule and to **nothing** under the rule its rows were written with. The three other worktree ledgers hold 1 row each, same story. The live `--dry-run` confirmed **0 files to import**.

- **Why the machinery went with it.** ~318 lines of concurrency-sensitive code (atomic claim-by-rename, orphan recovery, pid liveness, NUL enumeration, timestamp staleness, a five-value exit taxonomy) existed to migrate nothing, and generated roughly 20 of that PR's 23 review rounds. `B-195` and `B-197` closed alongside it: every race they recorded was a property of the migration, and with the migration gone there is no code left to race.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) BEFORE building any drain, re-run the measurement on the actual checkouts — reduce each `<worktree>/.harness/loop_status.md` under LEGACY semantics and count what is genuinely open. Zero means nothing to build; say so and stop. (2) Only a checkout that genuinely holds an open row warrants a drain, and then scope it to *that* case — the general cross-worktree form is what carried the concurrency surface. (3) The old files are untouched on disk and readable directly, so nothing is lost by not draining. (4) If a drain is ever built, read `B-195`/`B-197` first: they record the failure modes it will have to answer.

### B-199 · `merge_door._notify` cannot durably record a DEFERRED-HIL when every write fails *(surfaced repeatedly by out-of-family Codex across the U-HE-29 PR, 2026-08-22; register-and-held — raising would wedge the global merge-door lease, so release-safety has to come first)*

- **What it is.** C-HE-20 §1 makes a blocking escalation MUST-durable in the HITL queue and forbids a *new* escalation store. `_notify` retries a `DEFERRED-HIL` write 3× — which converts the common transient failure into the durable row the contract wants — and, if every attempt fails, prints a loud `ROW LOST` line naming the contract and returns. It does **not** raise.

- **Why it does not raise, which is a trade rather than an oversight.** This module has **no `finally:`** releasing the lease around the 8 `DEFERRED-HIL` call sites, so an exception escaping `_notify` can leave the **global** merge-door lease held — wedging every lane. That swaps a recoverable *reporting* failure for an unrecoverable *coordination* one. The residual is real and precisely bounded: a persistent write failure leaves the escalation only in that stderr line, invisible at the next SessionStart.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) Make the call sites release-safe FIRST — wrap the lease-holding region in `try/finally` so an exception cannot strand the lease; only then is propagation affordable. (2) Then propagate on the MUST-durable kind (`DEFERRED-HIL`) while keeping tolerance for the informational `NOTIFY`, which §1 itself distinguishes. (3) Do **not** add a second escalation store as a fallback — §1 forbids it, and the lease sidecar is not a HITL queue. (4) Witness release-safety directly (force a raise mid-landing, assert the lease is released), not by inferring it from tests that never raise.

### B-200 · C-HE-11 §1 per-lane telemetry endpoints — the lane's stack is isolated, its consumers still dial lane 0 *(surfaced by out-of-family Codex r2 against U-HE-31, 2026-08-23; registered, not blocking the unit)*

- **Current state.** REGISTERED, not blocking. U-HE-31 landed the isolation half in full (per-lane project name + the four host ports, witnessed); no consumer has been rewired yet, and nothing is scheduled ahead of the remaining S4 units.

- **What it is.** U-HE-31 gives lane `k >= 1` its own Compose project and its own host-port block, and the `R420_PORT_*` exports carrying those numbers live only inside the `r420-self-hosted-stack-{up,down,status}` child shells. Nothing else in the workspace reads them: the self-hosted config surface and the R-420 live-E2E recipes still name `4317` / `3200` / `3000` literally. A `k >= 1` lane therefore brings up a correctly ISOLATED stack that its own harness run does not talk to — it exports to lane 0's collector, or, with no lane 0 up, skips or fails.

- **Why it is not a defect in the landed unit.** C-HE-11 §1 is a contract about bringing the stack up without colliding: a per-lane `-p` project and the full host-port set `{3000, 3200, 4317, 4318}`. That half is met and witnessed. The CONSUMER half is not in the contract's text and not in the unit's Files list, so wiring it inside U-HE-31 would have been a silent scope extension. It is named here instead, which is what the 3–4-lane pilots (C-HE-13 §3) will need the moment a lane wants to read its own traces.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) Choose the carrier — a lane-aware OTLP endpoint resolved at config load from `HARNESS_LANE_INDEX` / `R420_PORT_OTEL_GRPC`, versus per-lane config files. (2) Thread it through the R-420 live-E2E recipes and `docs/how-to-deploy.md`, whose port literals are the other half of the gap. (3) Witness with a two-lane run whose traces land in that lane's OWN Tempo, not lane 0's. Blocked on nothing; scheduled behind the remaining S4 units.

### B-201 · C-HE-11 §2 `gc.auto 0` — warn-and-continue vs refuse-to-open when the shared git config cannot be written *(raised three times by out-of-family Codex against U-HE-31, 2026-08-23; register-and-held on the documented reading; CLOSED at U-HE-32, 2026-08-24)*

- **Current state.** CLOSED. The hold named exactly one close-out condition — U-HE-32's bounded retry — and it has landed. `tools/hooks/lane-init.sh` now writes `gc.auto 0` through `hook_git_retry` (C-HE-11 §3: full jitter over base 100 ms, factor 2, cap 5 s, 8 attempts), so the ordinary way this write loses — a concurrent lane holding `.git/config.lock`, which clears in milliseconds — no longer reaches the warning at all. What still warns-and-opens is the residue after an exhausted budget: a config that is genuinely unwritable rather than momentarily contended, where refusing every lane in the workspace over a hygiene knob remains the worse trade. The reviewer's objection was to an unretried MUST; there is no longer one. The refuse-vs-warn question for that NON-transient residue is not dropped with this closure — it is split to **B-205**, which is where it is now tracked.

- **What it is.** C-HE-11 §2 says `gc.auto 0` MUST be set repo-wide, once, idempotently by whichever lane-init runs first. `tools/hooks/lane-init.sh` attempts it, and when the write fails (a locked or unwritable shared config) it prints a named warning to stderr and the lane still opens. The reviewer's position, raised in rounds 4, 5 and 6, is that a failed MUST should refuse to open the lane.

- **Why it is held rather than absorbed.** Two things separate this from the other MUSTs in the same file, both of which DO fail closed (an unpersistable lane identity, an unallocatable lane index). First, its failure mode is bounded and named: automatic GC during concurrent lane work causes local ref/index lock contention, which is exactly what C-HE-11 §3's bounded retry helper covers — `hook_git_retry`, landing at U-HE-32, the very next unit. Second, the blast radius of failing closed is worse than the hazard: an unwritable git config would make every lane in the workspace un-openable over a hygiene knob, converting a degraded-but-workable environment into an unusable one. The failure is loud (stderr, named, pre-action), so nothing is silently absorbed.

- **Close-out record (U-HE-32).** (1) DONE — `hook_git_retry` bounds the contention, and the witness is `tools/hooks/test_lib.sh`'s config-lock case, which exists because git reports this shape as `could not lock config file …: File exists` with no `.lock` substring anywhere: the plan's own suggested pattern, written from the index/ref wording, would have missed the very write this row is about. (2) is not a residual of this row and needs nothing built — it is a conditional re-open: if the 3–4-lane pilots ever record a `cause_signature` naming lock contention recurring across runs (C-HE-13 §3), that is an ordinary pilot finding and fail-closed gets revisited then. (3) no further narrowing owed.

### B-202 · C-HE-11 §1/§5 lane-teardown and headroom residuals that need a primitive this unit does not have — a claim↔cleanup lock, and available-memory INSIDE the Docker VM *(surfaced by out-of-family Codex across U-HE-31 rounds 9–11, 2026-08-23; registered at the 11-round cap)*

- **Current state.** REGISTERED at U-HE-31's 11-round review cap. Every cheap fix around both residuals has landed; what remains needs a primitive outside this unit, and neither residual has been observed — both are reasoned.

- **What it is.** Two residuals. (1) **Claim↔cleanup interleaving.** `hook_release_lane_index` re-reads the claim's owner immediately before AND after `docker compose down --volumes`, so a rebind by a worktree recreated at that path is detected and its claim left alone. What the re-reads cannot do is un-destroy containers: if the rebind lands inside the gap between the pre-check and the compose call, the old release destroys the new owner's stack. Closing it needs a lock shared by the release path and lane-init's claim path — a primitive neither has, and one that would put a lock acquisition inside the worktree-removal hook. (2) **Available memory inside the Docker VM.** C-HE-11 §5 asks for "available memory / Docker-VM headroom". Lane-init checks the VM's `MemTotal` ceiling AND host availability, both against the stack's need; what no Docker API exposes is the VM's *free* memory. A VM sized adequately but already consumed passes both checks. Measuring it means running a probe container (`docker run --rm … free`), which needs an image pull inside a sourced shell hook.

- **Why it is registered rather than fixed here.** Both wanted a mechanism outside this unit's Files list, and rounds 9–11 converged on them precisely because the cheap fixes around them had all landed. Their blast radius is bounded: (1) needs a worktree reaped and recreated at the same path inside one teardown window; (2) surfaces as containers failing to start, at the moment of use, which is loud even if it is not the pre-flight refusal §5 prefers.

- **Third residual, added at round 15 after a fix for it was built and then backed out.** A lane reaped between its worktree's deletion and its claim's release leaves a claim nothing retries — that index is consumed for good. U-HE-31 tried to close this by letting the allocator reclaim any claim naming a path that no longer exists. Out-of-family review then showed the cure was worse: the reclamation deletes by pathname after an UNLOCKED observation, so two initializers seeing one dead claim can have the second's stale `rm` delete the first's newly published live claim (P1), and "the directory is absent" is not proof of death at all — the removal path MOVES a live worktree to quarantine and can restore it, so the scan reclaims a lane that is coming back. Both need the same claim↔cleanup lock as residual (1), which is why the reclamation was reverted rather than patched: an unlocked half-fix loses a live claim, where the leak it addressed only wastes an index. Whichever lock closes (1) closes this too — one primitive, three symptoms.

- **Fourth symptom, and the one that names the shape of the whole row.** The post-verify duplicate-claim withdrawal in `lane-init.sh` cannot enforce "one worktree, one claim" without the same lock. Three review rounds each defeated a lock-free rule with a new interleaving: a symmetric "the peer's stands, mine goes" has both racers delete and leaves ZERO claims; a two-way tie-break on the index leaves two standing under a three-way race, because `lanes/*` sorts lexicographically and the middle claim never compares against the true minimum; comparing against the MINIMUM fixes that but still cannot help a source whose scan runs before any peer has published — it sees no duplicate, keeps its claim unconditionally, never re-checks, and a later lower-index source then correctly declines to withdraw, so both stand. Each rule is strictly better than the last and none of them is sufficient, because scan-and-decide without synchronisation is not a consensus primitive. The minimum rule is retained (it converges every case where the racers see each other, and can never leave zero) and the code now states that bound instead of claiming the invariant.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) Give the lane registry a per-index lock (the `mkdir` primitive lane-init already uses for corpse repair) and take it in BOTH `hook_release_lane_index` and lane-init's claim path — one lock, three callers, since the post-verify withdrawal needs it too; (2) for headroom, decide between a probe container behind an explicit opt-in and treating the VM ceiling as the contract's practical reading, and record the decision against C-HE-11 §5; (3) the 3–4-lane pilots (C-HE-13 §3) are the measurement that says whether either is worth the mechanism — neither has been observed, both are reasoned.

### B-203 · `hook_git_retry` does not reach the skill-side lane git operations — a shell function cannot survive an agent's Bash tool call, and the guard does not admit a `source … && hook_git_retry …` shape *(surfaced by out-of-family Codex r1 against U-HE-32, 2026-08-24; registered, not blocking the unit)*

- **Current state.** REGISTERED at U-HE-32 and HELD through four out-of-family raises (r1, r2, r3, r4 — it was the ONLY finding left standing at r4, every other having been absorbed). The hold is not a disagreement with the observation, which is correct: the hook-side consumers named by the unit's Scope are wired, the skill-side ones are not, and a registration is not an implementation. It is a statement about ownership — the close-out needs two surfaces this unit does not touch, named below.

- **What it is.** C-HE-11 §3 says local ref/index lock collisions MUST be retried. `hook_git_retry` delivers that for every git mutation that runs *inside a hook script* — `lane-init.sh`'s `gc.auto 0` write and the two worktree mutations `safe-worktree-remove.sh` drives. It does not cover the git commands an *agent* runs from a skill: `ship-pr` and `two-lane` issue raw `git add`, `git commit` and `git worktree add`, and those contend for `index.lock` exactly like the wrapped ones do.

- **Why it is registered rather than fixed here.** Two mechanisms are missing, and neither is this unit's surface. (1) A shell function does not survive across an agent's Bash tool calls — each call is a fresh shell — which is the same reason `roadmap-continue/SKILL.md` tells an agent to restate `HARNESS_ARC_ID`/`HARNESS_LANE_ID` inline on every command rather than exporting them once. So a skill cannot simply be told to "call `hook_git_retry`"; the guidance would be inert. (2) The only shape that would work is a chained `source tools/hooks/lib.sh && hook_git_retry …`, and the permission guard auto-allows bare git but not that chain, so in loop mode every wrapped call would stall at ask-then-deny. Closing this needs a guard-allowlisted invocation shape — a permission-guard change, which is where U-HE-25's surface lives, not U-HE-32's.

- **Close-out steps, and who owns them.** (1) Decide the invocation shape — a `just` recipe is the obvious candidate, because a recipe name is a single clean token the guard can admit where a `source … && …` chain is not; (2) admit it in `tools/hooks/permission-guard.sh` with its own assertions — that is the **U-HE-25** surface, the reviewed permission-guard unit; (3) convert the raw git mutations in `ship-pr`/`two-lane` to it — that is the **U-HE-39** surface, the skill-carrier doc sweep, which also owes the wiring-suite update any `SKILL.md` change requires. Doing (2) and (3) inside U-HE-32 would be a silent scope extension across two other units' Files lists, which is the thing the plan's Files discipline exists to prevent.

- **Blast radius while it is open.** Bounded and loud. An unretried collision fails the agent's git command visibly, and the agent re-runs it; nothing is silently corrupted and no ledger row is lost. That is materially different from the hook-side case this unit did close, where the same collision happened inside an unattended script with no one to re-run it.

### B-204 · `reservations.py update --set` coerces a valid abbreviated sha to a float, so `head_sha=<hex that reads as scientific notation>` is refused as `inf` *(surfaced in-lane while back-filling U-HE-32's reservation, 2026-08-24; registered)*

- **Current state.** REGISTERED at U-HE-32.

- **What it is.** `uv run python tools/reservations.py update --arc-id u-he-32 --set head_sha=65106e2179` — a valid 10-character abbreviated sha — is refused with `head_sha must be a 7-64 char lowercase-hex sha/oid or null (C-HE-03 §3), got inf`. The `--set` parser coerces numeric-looking values before the validator sees them, and `65106e2179` is legal scientific notation (`65106 × 10^2179`), which overflows to `inf`. Any abbreviated sha of the form `<digits>e<digits>` hits it; the full 40-character form usually does not, because it almost always carries a non-`e` hex letter.

- **Why it matters more than the cosmetics suggest.** The failure is loud here, but it is loud only because the validator happened to reject `inf`. The same coercion runs over every `--set` value, so a field whose validator *accepts* a float would take the coerced value silently. It is also a shape that fails intermittently by content rather than by code path — the reason it surfaced at all is that one particular commit's short sha happened to read as a float.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) Keep `--set` values as strings and let each field's own validator do any conversion it wants; (2) add a case pinning `head_sha=<digits>e<digits>`, which is the fixture that would have caught it.

### B-205 · C-HE-11 §2 `gc.auto 0` — refuse-to-open vs warn-and-continue once the write fails a NON-transient way, i.e. after U-HE-32's retry is exhausted *(split out of B-201 at its closure so the surviving obligation stays tracked; out-of-family Codex r2 against U-HE-32, 2026-08-24)*

- **Current state.** REGISTERED. This is the half of B-201 that U-HE-32 did NOT settle, split to its own row so closing B-201 does not bury it (out-of-family Codex r2 made exactly this objection to the closure, and it was right).

- **What it is.** C-HE-11 §2 makes `gc.auto 0` a MUST. B-201 held on warn-and-continue with one named close-out: U-HE-32's bounded retry, which has now landed — `lane-init.sh` writes through `hook_git_retry`, so transient `.git/config.lock` contention no longer surfaces at all. The question that survives is narrower and genuinely different: when the write fails *after* an exhausted budget — an unwritable or corrupt shared config, not a peer lane holding the lock for milliseconds — should lane-init still open the lane?

- **Why it is a real question and not a formality.** Both readings have force. The MUST is unqualified, and every other MUST in `lane-init.sh` fails closed (an unpersistable lane identity, an unallocatable lane index). Against that: the blast radius of refusing is that an unwritable git config makes EVERY lane in the workspace un-openable over a hygiene knob, converting a degraded-but-workable environment into an unusable one — and the hazard `gc.auto 0` removes is itself lock contention, which `hook_git_retry` now absorbs. What separates this from B-201 is that the transient case is gone, so the decision is no longer being made against a failure mode that mostly was not real.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) The 3–4-lane pilots (C-HE-13 §3) are the measurement: a `cause_signature` naming lock contention recurring across runs says warn-and-continue is too permissive; its absence says the retry settled it. (2) Decide refuse-vs-warn against that evidence rather than against the unqualified MUST alone, and record the decision at C-HE-11 §2. (3) Nothing is owed before the pilots — this row exists so the question is not lost, not because work is queued behind it.

### B-206 · `hook_git_retry` inside the worktree-removal mutex can add up to ~23 s to a critical section whose waiters time out at 30 s *(surfaced by the merge-gate concurrency lens against U-HE-32, 2026-08-24; registered — the measurement is the close-out, not a code change)*

- **Current state.** REGISTERED at U-HE-32, and CORROBORATED INDEPENDENTLY. The sibling half of the same finding — the signal-handler path racing a 2 s SIGKILL — WAS fixed in the unit (the trap now restores fail-fast at one attempt). This half was reached separately by two decorrelated reviewers in the same round — the merge-gate concurrency lens and out-of-family Codex r5 — arriving at the SAME arithmetic (≤ 22.6 s of added sleeps against a 30 s waiter timeout) from different starting points. Agreement between decorrelated reviewers is the strongest confidence signal available here, so this row is a high-priority registration rather than a speculative one; what it still lacks is a measurement, not credibility.

- **What it is.** `hook_safe_worktree_remove` holds the worktree mutex from `tools/hooks/lib.sh:1024` to `:1123`, and BOTH retried git calls sit inside it: the `worktree move` at `:1077` and the `worktree remove` at `:1099`. Each can now spend a full C-HE-11 §3 budget — seven jittered waits with ceilings 100/200/400/800/1600/3200/5000 ms, so **≤ 11.3 s worst case, ~5.6 s expected**. Out-of-family review r7 sharpened the count: the RESTORE path is a third retried call inside the same span, so the worst case is **three** budgets, **≤ 33.9 s**, not two. That crosses a threshold — 22.6 s merely ate most of a waiter's allowance, 33.9 s **exceeds it outright**. Concurrent waiters on the same mutex — SessionStart lease registration at `:488`, `:526`, `:561` — block for `HARNESS_WORKTREE_LOCK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, default **30 s** (`:428`). So a removal that hits sustained contention can push a concurrent lease registration past its acquire timeout, where before this unit it could not — and at three budgets it does so with room to spare rather than marginally.

- **Why it is registered rather than fixed here.** The retry only ENGAGES under contention — with no collision it adds nothing, and the worst case needs sustained lock contention across two separate git operations, which is a machine already in trouble. Both plausible fixes are design changes rather than tuning: shrink the mutex span so the retried calls sit outside it, or make the budget lock-aware (a caller holding a mutex passes a smaller `HOOK_GIT_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, the seam the signal-handler fix already introduced). Picking between them without a measurement would be guessing, and *lowering* the budget inside the mutex would put a number below the C-HE-11 §3 MUST on a path the contract governs.

- **Relationship to B-202.** B-202 already owns the lane-registry lock work; this row is adjacent but distinct — B-202 is about a MISSING lock, this is about an EXISTING lock being held longer. If the B-202 lock work reshapes this critical section, close them together.

- **A third remedy, grounded while registering this row.** The 30 s bound is NOT contract-pinned — it appears nowhere in `Spec_HE_Loop_Lanes_v1.md`, only as a `${HARNESS_WORKTREE_LOCK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS:-30}` default at `tools/hooks/lib.sh:447` — so raising it is available without touching any MUST. It is NOT obviously right, which is why it is recorded rather than applied: a larger bound removes the spurious failure but makes a genuinely WEDGED holder that much slower to surface, and callers that deliberately pass 1 (`codex-session-end.sh:10`) show the value is already used as a policy knob rather than a constant. Which failure is worse is what the measurement below decides.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) During the 3–4-lane pilots (C-HE-13 §3), record whether any lease registration actually times out, and whether any `worktree move`/`remove` ever exhausts its budget at all — both are currently reasoned, neither observed; (2) if it fires, choose between shrinking the span and a lock-aware budget, and record the decision against C-HE-11 §3; (3) nothing owed before that measurement.

### B-207 · `hook_git_retry`'s stderr-capture temp file leaks when a signal trap `exit`s mid-retry *(surfaced and measured by the merge-gate concurrency lens against U-HE-32, 2026-08-24; registered — the lens itself judged it register-not-block)*

- **Current state.** REGISTERED at U-HE-32.

- **What it is.** `hook_git_retry` captures git's stderr to a `mktemp` file (`tools/hooks/lib.sh`, `errfile=$(mktemp)`) and removes it on the way out of the function. The removal is only reached by a normal `return`. `_hook_worktree_interrupted` terminates the process with `exit` straight from the HUP/INT/TERM trap, so a signal arriving while the retry is mid-backoff skips the cleanup and strands the file. Measured, not reasoned: the lens held `.git/index.lock` permanently, sent SIGTERM mid-backoff, and counted exactly one surviving suffix-less `tmp.*` entry under `$TMPDIR` (4353 → 4354).

- **Why it is registered rather than fixed.** One small file per INTERRUPTED teardown, in a directory the OS reaps; nothing about correctness, the retry contract, or the restore depends on it. The obvious fixes each cost more than the leak: an `EXIT` trap inside a library function would clobber whatever trap the caller installed (and `hook_safe_worktree_remove` installs three), and a deterministic per-PID path trades the leak for a predictable name in a shared temp directory. Note the leak became REACHABLE only because the trap now fires promptly — before the `sleep … & wait $!` fix the signal was deferred to the end of the sleep, so this is the small cost of a much larger correctness win.

- **Close-out steps.** (1) If a fix is wanted, the cheap shape is a per-invocation directory created under a caller-owned root and removed by the same code that owns the trap, rather than a trap inside the library; (2) otherwise close as WONTFIX once the pilots confirm no operator ever notices it. Nothing is owed before then.

### B-208 · the shared HITL loop ledger was reachable from a test process — 6288 of its 6589 rows were synthetic *(surfaced while clearing the U-HE-32 refresh gates, 2026-08-24; CLOSED at #1443 the same arc)*

- **Current state.** CLOSED at #1443, the arc that found it.

- **What it was.** `loop_status_path()` (`tools/hooks/loop_lib.sh:31`) resolves the loop ledger from the ambient environment and falls back to the operator's real `~/.gstack/projects/arhugula-v2/loop_status.md` whenever `HARNESS_LOOP_STATUS_PATH` is unset. Unset is the default state of every pytest process, so any test reaching a real emit path appended **real** `DEFERRED-HIL` rows to the venue the SessionStart hook reads. Measured on `main` at `e6913c112`: **6288** synthetic `lane=A` fixture rows and only **82** from real lanes, out of 6589 lines / 1.07 MB — deliberately *not* stated as a partition, since the balance is `lane=-` infra rows plus the file's own header (the first phrasing read as an exhaustive split and did not reconcile, 6288+82=6370; the round-5 lens caught it — the fourth claim in this arc to be checkable and wrong) — and a fabricated `pr-1 — pr #1: gh transport exploded` gate (pr #1, placeholder shas) nagging the operator at every session start. Because the ledger is append-only by contract (C-HE-09 §1, the single-file atomic-append guarantee; §2 is venue determinism), the debris is not removable after the fact; only a hand-written `RESOLVED-HIL` clears the nag.

- **How it was confirmed.** Reproduced, not inferred: running the single door test `test_raw_exception_after_attempt_blocks_lease` with `HARNESS_LOOP_STATUS_PATH` pointed at a scratch file emitted that exact nagging row into the scratch file — establishing both that the test really writes and that the environment variable is the lever.

- **Why the fix is not in `test_merge_door.py`.** Per-file isolation is what the workspace already tried and what drifted: `test_arc_exit_report.py` and `test_review_wrapper.py` remember to set the variable, `test_merge_door.py` does not, and a file written tomorrow will not either — correctness that depends on each author remembering an env var is ambient coupling, not a boundary. `test_merge_door.py` does monkeypatch `emit_loop_row` in most tests, so the hazard was seen; but several of its tests drive `merge_door.py` as a **real subprocess**, and monkeypatching a Python seam cannot cross a process boundary. Only the inherited environment reaches those, which is exactly why the enforcement belongs at the process boundary: one point for the whole directory, so no `tools/` test can reach the production ledger by omission. The first cut put it in the ROOT conftest and CI caught the over-reach — a root redirect leaks a `HARNESS_*` name into every axis suite, and `harness-runtime/tests/test_config_loader.py::test_env_defaults_to_os_environ_when_none` asserts that none is set, because RuntimeConfig's env loader consumes that namespace. Every loop-row producer lives under `tools/`, so that directory is the joint, and enforcing there keeps both invariants true instead of trading one for the other.

- **Witnesses.** `tools/test_loop_status_isolation.py`. One pins the redirect; the load-bearing one drives a real `emit_loop_row` (which shells out to `loop_log_structured`, the same writer the subprocess tests use) and asserts the row landed in the redirect. It is deliberately hermetic — it relocates the *computed fallback* to a tmp dir first, so reverting the fix sends the write into a file the test owns rather than reproducing the damage the fix prevents. Mutation-probed: commenting the redirect out reds both. The first cut read the env var by subscript and died with a `KeyError` before the emit ran, proving only that a variable was read; it was restructured to read defensively and assert the untouched-fallback claim first, so the probe now fails on the mechanism itself. Verified end to end: the full 119-test door suite left the operator's ledger byte-identical (1097455 bytes both sides).

- **Two out-of-family rounds, each finding a real defect in the fix rather than in the original code.** Round 1: the `mkdtemp` venue had no owner and accrued one temp tree per run — B-207's shape, reappearing in the thing written to fix a different leak. The re-home to a fixture gave it a teardown; measured 9 dirs before and 9 after, where it had grown by one. Round 2: the fixture was session-scoped, so `HARNESS_LOOP_STATUS_PATH` stayed set for everything running later *in the same process*, and a mixed `pytest tools/… harness-runtime/…` invocation failed the axis no-`HARNESS_*` invariant. That one was **confirmed by running it**, not conceded on argument — and it exposed a gap in my own verification, which had only ever exercised the two suites separately. The redirect is now per-test via `monkeypatch` over a session-scoped root, which makes the isolation a property rather than an ordering coincidence. Re-broadening it was, at that moment, structurally refused — a session-scoped fixture cannot request the function-scoped `monkeypatch` fixture, so pytest raised `ScopeMismatch`. That protection did NOT survive round 5: delegating to an independent `pytest.MonkeyPatch.context()` means the fixture no longer requests `monkeypatch` at all, so `scope="session"` became legal again and the third witness is now the only guard against it (re-verified by mutation at that point — the witness still reds). A claim that stops being true when a later round changes the mechanism is exactly the kind that rots, so it is corrected here rather than left standing. That third witness runs the mixed invocation in a subprocess, with `HARNESS_*` stripped from the child so it models a fresh run rather than inheriting the parent test's own redirect.

- **Round 3 — the fix walked into a trap this repo had already documented.** The per-test redirect rode on `monkeypatch`, which is ONE function-scoped instance shared between a test body and every fixture that requests it; `undo()` empties the whole stack, not just the caller's entries. Nine `tools/` tests call `monkeypatch.undo()` mid-test to drop a `run` stub *before* exercising the real subprocess runner, so the redirect would be lifted immediately before the emit that most needs it, and the row would resolve the operator's ledger. `test_arc_exit_report.py::shared_ledger` carries a comment saying exactly this and avoids it with an explicit save/restore — prior art the fix had not honoured. Found by out-of-family review and, independently, by CI, where that file's own pin was rolled back underneath the redirect and four tests failed with `FileNotFoundError`. Now an explicit `try/finally` around `os.environ`, with a fourth witness that performs the mid-test `undo()` and asserts the emit still lands in the redirect; mutation-probing it back to `monkeypatch` reds that witness *and* reproduces the four CI failures.

- **Round 4 — the merge-gate witness lens found half the round-3 fix untested.** Restoring an environment variable has two modes (it was set; it was not), and only one is reachable from a pytest process nobody pre-configured, so the hand-rolled `try/finally` shipped a restore branch no witness could reach. The lens confirmed it dead by mutation — replacing the teardown with an unconditional `pop` left both the new file (4/4) and `test_arc_exit_report.py` (92/92) green. Resolved by **deleting** the branch rather than contriving a witness for a path that only becomes observable after the process exits: an independent `pytest.MonkeyPatch.context()` owns both modes, and because it is a *separate* instance from the `monkeypatch` fixture, it stays immune to the mid-test `undo()` that round 3 was about. The same lens showed only the `[mine, axis]` order of witness 3 discriminates against a session-scope regression; that order is what catches it, the reverse order is kept because it alone catches a redirect established at import or collection time, and the docstring now says which is which instead of implying both do the same work.

- **Round 5 — the lens falsified a claim the previous round had just written.** Round 4 kept witness 3's reverse subprocess order on the grounds that it alone catches a redirect established at import or collection time. Probing that shape reds BOTH orders equally (1 failed, 1 passed each), because pytest imports every conftest before running any test — so the justification was simply wrong, and no regression shape was found that the reverse order uniquely catches. It is dropped rather than kept as ceremony whose stated reason does not hold. The same round surfaced a branch this arc *deadened elsewhere*: because the directory-level autouse redirect always sets up before module-level fixtures, `test_arc_exit_report.py::shared_ledger`'s own `prev is None` arm became unreachable (92/92 green with it dropped) — the exact untested-restore pattern round 4 had just removed, silently recreated in the file the arc keeps citing as prior art. That fixture now delegates to `MonkeyPatch.context()` as well, which removes the branch, keeps its documented immunity to a mid-test `undo()` (probed: 4 tests red without it), and stays correct if the conftest redirect ever goes away. Cleaning up an orphan this change created, not scope creep.

- **Round 6 — the fix for round 1 had gone three rounds without a witness.** The `shutil.rmtree` teardown that closes the `mkdtemp` accrual leak was never asserted by anything: deleting it left the new file and `test_arc_exit_report.py` entirely green. Session teardown cannot be observed from inside the session, so the fifth witness runs a child pytest with `TMPDIR` pointed at a directory it owns (`mkdtemp` honours it) and asserts nothing matching the venue prefix survives the child's exit. It is non-vacuous by construction: the child runs the redirect witness, which asserts the venue path contains the prefix, so its passing proves a directory *was* created under that `TMPDIR` — an empty survivor list therefore means removed, not never-made. Probed: deleting the teardown reds it, naming the surviving directory. The same round found witness 4's line citations stale by exactly two lines, shifted by this arc's **own** `shared_ledger` docstring edit the same day they were written. Correcting the numbers would only have reset the clock, so they were replaced by a count and a file list — which round 7 then found *also* false, and wrong on arrival rather than eventually (the real figures at that HEAD were fifteen sites across six files, including one the list never named). The paragraph now carries a bare `rg` invocation and no enumeration at all. Three representations rotted in this one arc — line numbers, a `ScopeMismatch` guarantee that a later round's own change invalidated, and a count — and each fix replaced one drifting map with another until the claim itself was removed. The durable rule the arc paid for: a fact checkable against HEAD does not belong in prose unless it is bound to a commit, because nothing redraws it.

- **Round 8 — the boundary was narrower than the claim.** The redirect was function-scoped, so it covered only test *bodies*: higher-scoped fixtures are set up before it and torn down after it, so anything emitting from a session- or module-scoped fixture still resolved the operator's ledger. Every witness through round 7 ran inside a test body, so none could see the gap. Grounding first showed it was not yet reachable — the only two session-scoped fixtures in `tools/` set an env var and scan for files — but the docstring claimed a boundary the mechanism did not deliver, and the honest options were to narrow the claim or widen the mechanism. Widened: a per-item `pytest_runtest_protocol` hookwrapper brackets setup, call and teardown together, so the whole lifecycle is covered while items outside `tools/` still never see the variable (round 2's property). **The path guard on that hookwrapper was measured, not assumed** — a subdirectory conftest's runtest hooks fire for items *anywhere* in the run, verified on a scratch tree, and an unguarded wrapper reintroduces the exact axis leak round 2 removed. Six witnesses then pinned six distinct properties (a round-8 figure — later rounds added more, and per this arc's own rule the current tally lives in the module, not in prose): dropping the guard reds only the axis-leak witness; reverting to a function-scoped fixture reds only the fixture-phase witness.

- **Round 9 — the cache guard was load-bearing and unwitnessed.** `_venue_root`'s `if _ROOT_KEY not in config.stash` is what makes one root serve the whole session. Deleting it left every witness then present green while stranding five directories per run — the exact B-207-shaped accrual round 1 exists to close. Witness 5 could not see it *by construction*: its child drove a single node id, and with one item "cached once" and "minted per item" are indistinguishable (both leave one directory, and `pytest_unconfigure` removes the one in the stash either way). The child now drives TWO items, chosen so neither spawns a child of its own — this test does, and naming the module would recurse. Verified: removing the cache reds it naming the survivor, and deleting the teardown still reds it too, so one witness now pins both halves of the accrual property.

- **Post-resume rounds (codex wrapper rounds 9–12, re-run at each new head).** Round 9: the module-phase witness called the real emitter without owning the computed fallback first, so in the exact regressed world it detects, its own setup would have polluted the operator ledger before the assertion fired — the observation is now captured first and the emit runs under an owned fallback (two-arm probe under a scratch HOME: old fixture reproduces the damage, fixed fixture leaves it absent, detection preserved). Round 10 demanded the phases outside the per-item bracket be witnessed; round 11 then showed per-scenario witnessing never converges (a session fixture in a module the canary child never imports slips every canary). Closed at the one joint every scenario shares instead: `pytest_configure` owns `ARC_METRICS_QUEUE_DIR` — the input `loop_status_path()` computes its fallback from, a documented override seam (C-HE-05) — for the whole session, so import time, collection, any-scope teardown and un-isolated child processes resolve an owned belt directory (every consumer but one — next bullet); a probe matrix measured each layer load-bearing (an inserted session-teardown emit and an inserted import-time emit each red their canary with the belt disabled and are absorbed with it on; module-scope teardown proved BRACKETED — pytest tears down to the next item's level inside the current item's teardown phase — so the reviewer's module-scope scenario was narrowed to session scope by measurement). Round 12: APPROVE. Full tools suite under the belt: 1719 passed, with the axis `HARNESS_*`-empty invariant green in a mixed run.

- **The 3-lens merge gate on the belt round.** The witness-adequacy lens caught two recurrences of this arc's own defect classes: the belt had only a presence witness (deleting its `setenv` red nothing behavioral), and its hand-rolled two-armed env restore reprised the exact round-4 shape whose dead arm was deleted rather than witnessed. Absorbed the same way as their ancestors: the restore now delegates to a stashed `MonkeyPatch` whose `undo()` at `pytest_unconfigure` owns both prior states, a behavioral witness lifts the bracket and asserts the real shell writer resolves the belt-derived fallback (reading the variable by subscript, so a belt-deletion probe reds before any emit can run), and a driver calls the configure/unconfigure pair directly to witness the restore in both prior states — the observation a live session structurally cannot make. All three probed to a kill. The spec-conformance lens caught this register itself stale at head — the belt rounds unnarrated and the round-8 witness count reading as current state — which this entry now corrects, plus the §2→§1 append-cite fix across carriers.

- **Rounds 13–15 — the belt carved, hardened, and converged.** Round 13 (P1): `ARC_METRICS_QUEUE_DIR` names TWO authorities — the ledger-fallback input and the LIVE lane registry — and the belt had demoted both, so the Docker lane test's destructive-teardown collision claims silently ran against a throwaway registry. The belt now preserves the demoted production value at `ARC_METRICS_QUEUE_DIR_PREBELT` and the lane test resolves through `production_queue_dir()` (PREBELT, else the home default — never the ambient variable, which under pytest IS the belt). Round 14 (P1): a nested pytest session — exactly what the canary children spawn — re-derived PREBELT from the parent's belt; publication is now first-writer-wins, the outermost capture being the authority, witnessed by the 7c driver's third arm. Round 15 (P2): the belt-implied fallback file and the bracket venue were two files, splitting a session's rows against C-HE-09 §2's one-venue reduction; the belt now sits directly under the venue root so both mechanisms name one ledger, pinned by an equality assert in 7a. Round 16: APPROVE. Every fix probe-killed both ways.

- **Gate round 2 (at the converged head).** Concurrency and witness-adequacy: APPROVE — the mid-arm-failure hazard in the 7c driver traces to a self-healing outcome through pytest's live-value `undo` semantics. Spec-conformance: BLOCK on exactly this register lagging rounds 13–15 (the round-12 belt sentence had become false once the round-13 carve-out existed) — corrected in this entry. One named residual is tracked rather than fixed-and-re-reviewed: the 7c driver leaks its own `mkdtemp` root when an arm fails mid-flight — bounded to already-failing runs, judged non-blocking by both code lenses, and left so the reviewed code stays byte-identical to its verdicts.

- **Deliberately not done.** The 6288 rows already in the ledger are not removed. It is append-only by contract and is operator state outside this repo, so truncating it is the operator's call, not this arc's; the pending synthetic gate was cleared the contract-sanctioned way, with a `RESOLVED-HIL` row.

### B-228 · selection-time disjointness gate reads committed heads — two fresh lanes on the same main always pass it *(surfaced by codex r2/r6/r7 on u-he-36, 2026-09-02; REGISTERED)*

- **What it is.** C-HE-13 §5 (spec v1.7) has `tools/arc_disjoint_check.py check --candidate HEAD` merge-tree the candidate against every other lane's live head BEFORE the lane reserves. At selection the candidate is `main`, so two lanes branching from the same main that will later edit the same hunk both pass; the collision surfaces at landing via `BASE_TOCTOU` (C-HE-12), which §5 names as the complement. Codex raised this in r2, r6 and r7 of the U-HE-36 PR as "not actual-write enforcement"; each time it was refuted on the contract's own text and the limit was named in the tool docstring, both carriers, and `test_check_reads_committed_tips_only`.
- **Current state.** OPEN, held. The mitigation on the same PR: the identical gate runs a SECOND time at ship-pr pre-flight (both carriers), when the candidate carries the arc's commits — a real textual conflict with a live sibling surfaces before the PR opens rather than at the door. The selection-time call keeps the spec's semantics.
- **Closure shape.** A spec-level decision (v1.8 note): (a) ratify the two-site shape (selection + ship pre-flight + landing BASE_TOCTOU) as §5's meaning and close; or (b) define a declared-scope carrier the gate can merge-tree against at selection — a design extension (X-AL-3) needing its own unit. Further review rounds cannot close it.

### B-231 · gate-log rows carry no failover-child marker — a gemini round cannot be told from a standalone review *(surfaced by codex r6/r7 on b-230-task-0, 2026-09-03; REGISTERED)*
